name: Live Formative Checks
title: Live Formative Checks
answer: Live formative checks are quick, low stakes assessments during a lesson, such as mini whiteboard questions or short online polls, that show a teacher whether students understand before moving on. AI can group the responses so patterns are visible at a glance, but the real value lies in what the teacher does next. They matter because a check that is collected and never acted on is wasted class time.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: Live formative checks are brief assessments woven into the middle of a lesson rather than saved for the end of a unit. They solve the problem of teaching forward without knowing whether students have actually followed, which leaves gaps to surface later when they are harder to fix. A quick question on a mini whiteboard or a short online poll gives the teacher a snapshot of the room in seconds, and tools such as Google Forms can collect those answers almost instantly. AI can then help group the responses so the teacher sees patterns at a glance instead of reading every answer one by one. The idea is not the collection itself but the speed of the signal, which lets teaching adjust while the lesson is still happening.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a teacher pauses partway through a lesson and asks students to answer a question on a mini whiteboard or through a short online poll. The responses come back in seconds, and AI can sort them into groups so the teacher can see at a glance where the class stands. If most students missed the question, the teacher reteaches right away rather than pressing on. If only a few missed it, the teacher works with those students while the rest move ahead. The text does not give grade band variations, so the practice applies across year groups as a routine part of a lesson.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label, study, figure or finding for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, describing what teachers can do with quick checks and how AI can help group responses. The claims about value are practical ones, tied to the teacher's next move rather than to measured outcomes.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Live checks must stay low stakes so students feel free to show what they do not understand without fear of a grade. The purpose is information for teaching, not a score for the gradebook, and students who trust the process are more honest about their confusion. The decision about what to do next stays with the teacher, who reteaches, pulls a small group, or moves the class on. A check that is collected and never acted on is wasted class time, so the tool only helps if a person responds to what it shows.
